items.stem:
Paper 1 – Guided textual analysis (SL: 1 hour 15 minutes for one text; HL: 2 hours 15 minutes for two texts).

Read the following home-front poster from a fictional wartime nation, written in the style of 1940s propaganda.

[Image: a woman in overalls rolls up her sleeve beside a factory gate; behind her, the silhouettes of marching soldiers.]
THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT.
YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE.
Every shell you make is a letter home.
Don't let them down – report for factory work today.

Guiding question: How does the poster persuade women to take up factory work?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the poster recruits by equating industrial labour with the soldier's heroism and with love. (1) Parallel capitals equate front and lathe. (2) The metaphor "a letter home" transforms shells into affection. (3) The image of the rolled sleeve models readiness, and the imperative uses guilt. Evaluation: the empowerment is conditional – it serves the war effort rather than women's equality.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: the poster recruits by equating industrial labour with the soldier's heroism and with love. (1) Parallel capitals equate front and lathe. (2) The metaphor "a letter home" transforms shells into affection. (3) The image of the rolled sleeve models readiness, and the imperative uses guilt. Evaluation: the empowerment is conditional – it serves the war effort rather than women's equality. Paper 1 criteria (5 marks each, 20 total). A Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the literal and implied meaning, references well chosen. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. C Focus and organisation: a clear line of argument that answers the guiding question (or a chosen focus) and is developed coherently. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.

Read the following extract from a travel brochure for a tour of Iceland.

Where fire meets ice. Stand where continents drift apart at Thingvellir. Soak beneath the northern lights in steaming geothermal pools. Let the silence of a black-sand beach rewrite your idea of quiet. This isn't a holiday. It's a reset. Small groups. Expert local guides. Carbon-offset flights.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "Compare the ways in which two works you have studied present a character's struggle with identity."

Write a comparative thesis statement and a three-point outline for an essay that answers this question with reference to two literary works you have studied.
items.answer: Model thesis: Both works present identity as negotiated between two cultures, but Satrapi visualises the split self through the shifting drawn image of Marji, while Lahiri locates the struggle in a name – Gogol – whose meaning the protagonist must grow into. Outline: (1) visual self-representation (the veil, the changing body) versus the motif of naming; (2) family as anchor and pressure in both; (3) endings: departure from Iran versus Gogol reading the Gogol book his father gave him.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "How do two works you have studied use humour or irony to make a serious point?"

With reference to two works you have studied, write two comparative body paragraphs that analyse how each writer's choices shape meaning and evaluate their effects.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis and Voltaire's Candide (in translation) – both use comic naivety to expose violence and ideology.) Thesis: Both works use a naïve perspective to make horror visible, but Satrapi's child narrator generates gentle, poignant humour, whereas Voltaire's satirical narrator turns Pangloss's optimism into absurdity. Points: the naïve viewpoint (young Marji versus Candide); visual comedy versus verbal irony; the serious target: political repression versus philosophical optimism. Evaluate whether humour softens or sharpens the critique.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "In what ways do two works you have studied present the abuse of power?"

Write the comparative analysis section of your essay: develop two integrated comparative points, each analysing specific authorial choices in both works.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four and Shakespeare's Macbeth – a totalitarian state and a tyrant.) Thesis: Both works show power corrupting truth and life, but Shakespeare locates abuse in one man's ambition and conscience, while Orwell depicts an impersonal system – Big Brother, Newspeak, Room 101 – that abuses power to control thought itself. Points: individual versus systemic power; language: Macbeth's equivocation versus Newspeak; outcome: restoration of order versus Winston's defeat. Evaluate which vision is more pessimistic and why.

Paper 1 – Guided textual analysis (SL: 1 hour 15 minutes for one text; HL: 2 hours 15 minutes for two texts).

Read the following pair of headlines and opening lines from two newspapers reporting the same student protest.

Newspaper A: 'Thousands of students march for affordable housing' – Students filled the city centre on Saturday, chanting and carrying handmade banners, to demand rent controls.
Newspaper B: 'Student mob brings city centre to standstill' – Shoppers were left stranded on Saturday as crowds of students blocked roads, causing chaos for local businesses.

Guiding question: How do the two newspapers shape readers' opinions of the same event?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the same facts are framed as civic action (A) and disruption (B). (1) Diction: "march" versus "mob". (2) Whose perspective is centred. (3) A includes the demand; B omits it. Evaluation: neither is strictly false; framing operates through selection and connotation.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "In what ways and to what effect do two works you have studied present the tension between individual desire and social expectation?"

With reference to two works you have studied, write two comparative body paragraphs that analyse how each writer's choices shape meaning and evaluate their effects.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House (studied in translation) and F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby – both centre a character whose desires collide with the codes of a class-conscious society, but one is drama and the other first-person retrospective narration, which allows a contrast of form.) Thesis: Both works dramatise desire constrained by social codes, but where Ibsen moves Nora towards a self-assertive break that the audience witnesses directly, Fitzgerald filters Gatsby's desire through Nick's retrospective narration so that it becomes a doomed, elegiac illusion. Points: symbols of desire and constraint: Nora's forbidden macaroons and the stripped Christmas tree versus Gatsby's green light; form: stage directions and the audience's direct view of Nora versus Nick's mediating, partly admiring narration; endings: the slammed door as liberation versus "boats against the current" as defeat. A strong answer evaluates how genre shapes the reader's judgement: the play invites the audience to judge society, the novel to mourn the dreamer.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "How and to what extent do two works you have studied use the perspective of an outsider?"

Write the comparative analysis section of your essay: develop two integrated comparative points, each analysing specific authorial choices in both works.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis (in translation) and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein – both centre a being excluded from family and society because of his form.) Thesis: Kafka and Shelley both use the excluded body to critique the community that rejects it, but Kafka keeps us close to Gregor's bewildered consciousness until his death, while Shelley grants the creature his own embedded narrative, making his eloquence an indictment of his creator. Points: narrative position: close third person in Kafka versus nested first-person narratives in Shelley; the family's response: the Samsas' relief versus Victor's abandonment; the outsider's voice: Gregor's loss of speech versus the creature's articulate self-education. Judge the extent: in both, the outsider becomes the moral centre, but Shelley makes the outsider's voice heard more fully.

Read the following infographic from an international water charity, described in words.

[Title in bold blue capitals: 'THE WALK'.] [A single dotted line runs right across the page and ends at a small well icon.]

Below: '20 litres. That's what she carries back – about the weight of a full suitcase.'
[Bottom panel: a tap icon.] 'A donation of 25 euros helps bring a tap within 15 minutes of her home.'

Guiding question: How does the infographic use visual and verbal features to persuade its audience?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the infographic converts statistics into a journey the reader can imagine. (1) The dotted line visualises distance. (2) The suitcase comparison and "she" personalise data. (3) The tap icon and specific donation make the solution feel achievable. Evaluation: effective, but risks representing women only as victims.

Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "How do two works you have studied use structure to create tension?"

With reference to two works you have studied, write two comparative body paragraphs that analyse how each writer's choices shape meaning and evaluate their effects.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Gabriel García Márquez's Chronicle of a Death Foretold (in translation) and Shakespeare's Macbeth – both announce or prophesy the outcome early.) Thesis: Both works generate tension not from what will happen but from how and why, yet García Márquez reveals Santiago Nasar's death in the first sentence and reconstructs it like an investigation, while Shakespeare uses the witches' prophecies to create a dread that the tragedy steadily fulfils. Points: early revelation versus prophecy; fragmented, retrospective investigation versus tightly compressed five-act tragedy; the effect of inevitability: collective guilt versus individual damnation. Evaluate whether knowing the end reduces or increases tension.
